title: find, grep, sed, and awk together
subtitle: Stop reading files one at a time. Locate the right evidence, filter it, transform it, and leave a report another operator can use.
objectives: Find files by name, type, and location without crossing unrelated trees
Search file contents recursively with grep and a safe pattern
Transform matching text with sed without rewriting the source
Select and reformat fields with awk
Produce a small evidence report through a pipeline

ex200.evidence: find with -type and -name on a bounded tree.
Pipeline writes a verified report file.

versionNotes: RHEL 9 and RHEL 10 ship GNU findutils, grep, sed, and gawk with the same core behavior used here.
RHEL 10 may ship newer versions with additional options. Prefer portable POSIX options in scripts that must also run on RHEL 9.

lab.title: From log noise to a short report
lab.scenario: Use the sandbox logs to find files, extract authentication failures, transform the unit name, and build two small reports under /tmp.

steps.text: Find regular log files under /var/log without leaving that tree.
steps.verify: The results are regular files under /var/log and include at least one .log file.
The output contains the failed-password lines with line numbers if -n is used.

steps.text: Create a transformed copy of the auth log with sshd replaced by auth.
steps.verify: The report exists and contains [auth] tags while the source file is unchanged.

steps.text: Use awk to list local human users and their UIDs.
steps.verify: The report contains student and its UID, with no system accounts.

steps.text: Build a short summary that another operator can read.
steps.cmd: printf "auth failures: " > /tmp/auth-summary.txt; sudo grep -c "Failed password" /var/log/secure >> /tmp/auth-summary.txt; printf "local users: " >> /tmp/auth-summary.txt; cat /tmp/local-users.txt | wc -l >> /tmp/auth-summary.txt
steps.verify: The summary contains both counts and is written under /tmp.

quiz.q: Which find expression limits results to regular files named *.log?
quiz.why: -type f selects regular files and -name matches the basename pattern.

quiz.q: What does sed "s/old/new/g" do by default?
options: Prints a changed view to stdout without modifying the file
quiz.why: sed writes to stdout unless -i is supplied; -i edits in place and should be used deliberately.
-F: sets the field separator, so $3 is the third field of each record.
